mcqs.question: Why is the worst case the default answer expected in interviews?
options: It is the easiest of the three cases to compute
It is the only case that gives a guarantee, independent of what the input looks like
It is the case that occurs most often on real data
The average case is undefined for most algorithms
mcqs.explanation: Worst case bounds every possible input, so it is a promise you can design an SLO around; the average is usually more representative of typical data but guarantees nothing about any particular request. Average case is well-defined once you state a distribution — the issue is that the distribution is an assumption.

mcqs.question: Textbook quicksort using the first element as pivot is given an already-sorted array. What happens?
options: It runs in O(n) because no swaps are needed
It runs in O(n log n) as usual, since sorting order does not affect partitioning
It degrades to O(n²) because every partition splits off just one element
It fails to terminate
mcqs.explanation: With the smallest value chosen as pivot every time, each partition peels off a single element and recursion depth becomes n, giving the quadratic worst case. Sorted input is extremely common in practice, which is exactly why real implementations randomize or median-of-three the pivot.

mcqs.question: A candidate says "hash map lookup is O(1)." What is the most useful correction?
options: That is the average case; the worst case is O(n) when keys collide into one bucket
It is O(log n), because hash maps are implemented as trees
It is O(1) only when the map holds fewer than a thousand keys
It is O(n) in all cases because the hash must be computed
mcqs.explanation: Constant-time lookup is an expectation over well-distributed keys; adversarial or poorly-hashed keys can pile into a single bucket and turn the probe into a linear scan. Computing the hash is O(1) in the key size, not O(n) in the number of entries.

mcqs.question: You are choosing a sort for a request path with a strict p99 latency SLO. Why might heapsort beat quicksort here despite quicksort's better constants?
options: Heapsort uses less memory, which lowers latency
Quicksort cannot sort data that arrives out of order
Heapsort is O(n log n) in every case, so it has no input-dependent spike to blow the p99
Heapsort has a better average-case complexity than quicksort
mcqs.explanation: Tail latency is governed by the worst case, and quicksort's O(n²) path — however rare — lands in the p99 rather than averaging away. Their average complexities are the same class; heapsort simply trades some constant-factor speed for the guarantee.

mcqs.question: What makes an average-case data structure a potential denial-of-service risk?
options: It consumes more memory than a worst-case structure
Its complexity is undefined when input is attacker-controlled
It cannot be used behind a load balancer
An attacker who controls the input can deliberately construct the worst case and burn CPU with a single request
mcqs.explanation: Average-case guarantees assume inputs are not chosen adversarially, and hash-collision floods or catastrophic regex backtracking break that assumption on purpose. The standard mitigation is randomizing the structure's behavior per process so collisions cannot be precomputed.
